										<content:encoded><p>A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/polly/">Amazon Polly</a> Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.</p> 
<p><img style="border: solid 1px #ccc" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/23/genai-agronegocio-speaker-crop-1280.jpg" alt="Presenting a session titled GenAI no Agronegocio Brasileiro to a group of agribusiness leaders seated around a boardroom table at the AWS office in Sao Paulo"></p> 
<p><em>Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.</em></p> 
<p>The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…</p> 
<p><strong>AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available</strong><br> AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.</p> 
<p>The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/">PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry</a> dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/using-aws-waf-to-apply-mitigations-for-php2shell-rce-vulnerabilities-cve-2026-109618-and-cve-2026-109619/">AWS WAF mitigations</a> for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).</p> 
<p><strong>Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway</strong><br> Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.</p> 
<p>The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.</p> 
<p><strong>Last week’s launches</strong><br> Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/amazon-polly-delivers-a-major-upgrade-to-its-generative-engine/">Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine</a> – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/aws-announce-native-pytorch-support-trainium">AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta)</a> – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-insights/your-last-hardware-decision-shouldnt-decide-what-you-build-next/">AWS Insights piece on that theme</a> is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/aws-announce-neuron-2-33-0">AWS Neuron 2.33</a>.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/announcing-new-ways-to-customize-models-with-sagemaker-ai-without-managing-gpus/">New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs</a> – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/write-your-own-training-loop-without-managing-gpus-with-amazon-sagemaker-training-sessions/">full technical walkthrough</a>, the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/training-session-apis-on-sagemaker-ai">training session APIs</a>, and new support for <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/amazon-sagemaker-muse-qwen-ministral/">Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3</a>.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/claude-structured-outputs-bedrock/">Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock</a> – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/amazon-elasticache-serverless-valkey-online-migration/">Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime</a> – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.</p> 
<p><strong>Other AWS news</strong><br> Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/discover-tools-at-runtime-with-aws-agent-registry/">Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry</a> – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-cloud-financial-management/tokenomics-for-coding-agents-benchmark-cost-and-quality-on-your-own-code/">Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code</a> – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/how-u-s-bank-migrated-119-tb-from-oracle-exadata-to-amazon-rds-for-oracle/">How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle</a> – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.</p> 
<p><strong>Upcoming AWS events</strong><br> Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.</p> 
<p><a href="https://reinvent.awsevents.com/">AWS re:Invent</a> – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.</p> 
<p><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/events/community-day/">AWS Community Days</a> – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.</p> 
<p>That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!</p> 
<p>– Daniel</p> 
<p><em>This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!</em></p></content:encoded>

		<link>https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/aws-continuum-for-code-vulnerabilities-is-now-generally-available/</link>
					
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Esra Kayabali]]></dc:creator>

					<description>AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is a new security service that uses AI to automatically find, validate, and prioritize code vulnerabilities in your environment, then delivers ready-to-review fixes as pull requests replacing what previously took hours of manual investigation and days of cross-team coordination.</description>
										<content:encoded><p>Today, we’re announcing the general availability of <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/continuum/">AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities</a>. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.</p> 
<p>Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.</p> 
<p>Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.</p> 
<p>Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.</p> 
<p>For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.</p> 
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in action<br> </strong></span>To show how this works, I open <a href="https://console.aws.amazon.com/continuum/home">AWS Continuum</a> in the console and go to <strong>Code vulnerabilities</strong>. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum <a href="http://docs.aws.amazon.com/continuum/latest/userguide/what-is-continuum.html">User Guide</a>.</p> 
<p>The <strong>Overview</strong> page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my <strong>Code integrations</strong>, the <strong>Environments</strong> built on them, and the status of any <strong>AWS collector</strong> that supplies AWS resource context.</p> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="alignnone wp-image-106064 size-full" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/19/1218373720644947-1.png" alt="" width="3032" height="1416"></p> 
<p>I open one of my environments. The <strong>Issues</strong> tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.</p> 
<p><a href="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-2c.png"><img loading="lazy" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-106112" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-2c.png" alt="" width="2462" height="2580"></a></p> 
<p>The <strong>Overview</strong> rates it High severity, with the status <strong>Completed</strong> and the remediation already <strong>Delivered</strong> to GitHub. The <strong>Risk assessment</strong> explains why. Continuum rates its <strong>Exploitability</strong> as <strong>Exploitable</strong>, with an evidence level of <strong>Static proven</strong> and a validation run status of <strong>Completed</strong>. <strong>Likelihood</strong> is <strong>High</strong>, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. <strong>Impact</strong> is <strong>Moderate</strong>, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A <strong>Proof</strong> section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.</p> 
<p>The <strong>Remediation</strong> section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled <strong>Continuum fix</strong>, and I choose <strong>View pull request</strong> to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A <strong>Contributing</strong> findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.</p> 
<p><a href="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-3c.png"><img loading="lazy" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-106106" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-3c.png" alt="" width="2462" height="3812"></a></p> 
<p>The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.</p> 
<p><a href="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-4c.png"><img loading="lazy" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-106108" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-4c.png" alt="" width="3032" height="3394"></a></p> 
<p>The <strong>Findings</strong> tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from.</p> 
<p><a href="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-5c.png"><img loading="lazy" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-106114" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/22/1218373720644947-5c.png" alt="" width="3032" height="2620"></a></p> 
<p>The <strong>Scans</strong> tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use <strong>Configure scan frequency</strong> to change the cadence or <strong>Queue scan</strong> to run one on demand. The <strong>Configuration</strong> tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.</p> 
<p>In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.</p> 
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Now available</strong></span><br> AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon)&nbsp;Regions. For pricing, visit the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/continuum/pricing">pricing page</a>.</p> 
<p>To learn more, visit the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/continuum/">AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page</a> and the <a href="http://docs.aws.amazon.com/continuum/latest/userguide/what-is-continuum.html">User Guide</a>. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.</p> 
<a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/esrakayabali/">— Esra</a></content:encoded>

					<description>Try Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.</description>
										<content:encoded><p>When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ecs/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS)</a>, configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/application-load-balancer/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">Application Load Balancers (ALBs)</a>, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/certificate-manager/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)</a> certificates, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/waf/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">AWS WAF</a> web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.</p> 
<p>Today, we’re announcing <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ecs/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">Amazon ECS Gateway</a>, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.</p> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-106076" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/20/2026-ECS-Gateway-architecture.png" alt="" width="1675" height="977"></p> 
<p>ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><strong>Platform teams</strong> create and configure a gateway, defining organizational networking standards including subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and WAF web ACLs, in a single place. They then associate the gateway with one or more ECS clusters, making it available to services running on those clusters.</li> 
 <li><strong>Application teams</strong> opt their services in by adding a gateway connector parameter when creating or updating a service. ECS provisions the required per-service resources automatically: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, target groups, and a service security group that permits inbound traffic only from the ALB. No networking expertise required.</li> 
</ul> 
<p>ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.</p> 
<p><strong><u>A first look at ECS Gateway</u></strong><br> In the <a href="https://console.aws.amazon.com/ecs/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">ECS console</a>, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.</p> 
<p>Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under <strong>Additional Settings</strong>, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.</p> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-105491" style="border: solid 1px #ccc" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/09/02/2026-ecs-gateway-1-create.jpg" alt="" width="1719" height="2560"></p> 
<p>Using <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/cli/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)</a>, call <code>CreateGateway</code> with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.</p> 
<pre><code class="lang-bash">aws ecs create-gateway \
  --name my-team-gateway \
  --infrastructure-role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ECSGatewayRole \
  --configuration '{
    "HostSharedAlb": {
      "networkConfiguration": {
        "subnets": [
          "subnet-080779f9bd887757a",
          "subnet-03d5b2fead6bc6258",
          "subnet-0861210a397d31252",
          "subnet-06539e194023cb77a"
        ],
        "ipAddressType": "ipv4"
      },
      "scheme": "internet-facing"
    }
  }'
</code></pre> 
<p>Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.</p> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-105492" style="border: solid 1px #ccc" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/09/02/2026-ecs-gateway-1-create-2.jpg" alt="" width="1800" height="978"></p> 
<p>Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.</p> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-105493" style="border: solid 1px #ccc" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/09/02/2026-ecs-gateway-2-connect.jpg" alt="" width="1800" height="1148"></p> 
<p>Use <code>AssociateGatewayWithCluster</code> to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:</p> 
<pre><code class="lang-bash">aws ecs associate-gateway-with-cluster \ 
--gateway my-team-gateway \ 
--cluster arn:aws:ecs:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/my-cluster</code></pre> 
<p>To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">AWS MCP Server</a> and <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/plugins.html?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">plugins</a> with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/gateway-overview.html?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">Amazon ECS Gateway documentation</a>.</p> 
<p><strong>ECS Gateway:Behind the scenes<br> </strong>A gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.</p> 
<p>Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.</p> 
<p>Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in <code>CreateService</code> or <code>UpdateService</code>. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling <code>UpdateService</code> to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.</p> 
<pre><code class="lang-bash">aws ecs create-service \ 
  --cluster my-cluster \ 
  --service my-api-service \ 
  --task-definition my-api-service:1 \ 
  --gateway-connectors '[{ "portName": "api", "filters": {"accessTypes": ["PUBLIC"]}, "healthCheck": {...} }]'</code></pre> 
<p>At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.</p> 
<p>For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to <code>maxAlbCount</code> referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes <code>ACTIVE</code>, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.</p> 
<p>ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><strong>Redeployments</strong>: On each deployment, ECS re-evaluates gateway associations. If new compatible gateways have been associated since the last deployment, your service connects to them. If a gateway has been disassociated, your service disconnects and the route is removed. Your service always reflects the current state of the cluster gateways at deployment time.</li> 
 <li><strong>Service deletion</strong>: ECS automatically disconnects the service from every gateway, removes all gateway routes, and cleans up all per-service resources. If the service held the last route on an ALB, that ALB is deprovisioned.</li> 
</ul> 
<p><strong>Things to Know</strong><br> Here are a few important details to keep in mind:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><strong>Networking</strong>: ECS Gateway is available for ECS services using the <code>awsvpc</code> network mode across all launch types (Amazon ECS EC2, AWS Fargate, and ECS Managed Instances). Your service Availability Zones (AZs) must be a subset of each gateway’s AZs on the cluster. A gateway ALB only routes traffic to tasks in AZs where it has subnets. We recommend creating gateways and services for a given cluster with the same set of AZs.</li> 
 <li><strong>Capacity</strong>: If <code>maxAlbCount</code> is reached and no ALB has available capacity, the deployment fails. Default quota limit of <code>maxAlbCount</code> is 10. Plan your <code>maxAlbCount</code> setting according to the number of services you expect to connect.</li> 
 <li><strong>Observability</strong>: Use ALB metrics in CloudWatch with the <code>TargetGroup</code> dimension to monitor per-service traffic, and <code>LoadBalancer</code> dimension to monitor traffic across the shared ALB. Use <code>describe-target-health</code> to check real-time target status. Configure CloudWatch alarms for metrics such as <code>HealthyHostCount</code>, <code>TargetResponseTime</code>, and <code>HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count</code>, using gateway ARN-based tagging so monitoring scales automatically with your <code>maxAlbCount</code>.</li> 
</ul> 
<p><strong><u>Now available</u></strong><br> Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ecs/pricing/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">Amazon ECS Pricing page</a>.</p> 
<p>To get started,&nbsp;create your first gateway today in the <a href="https://console.aws.amazon.com/ecs/?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">ECS console</a>, and&nbsp;send feedback to <a href="https://repost.aws/tags/TAefn4YSprR-uCBYmbofOpHw/amazon-elastic-container-service?trk=d8ec3b19-0f37-4f8c-8c12-189f913e205c&amp;sc_channel=el">AWS re:Post for ECS</a> or through your usual AWS Support contacts.</p> 
<p>— <a href="https://linkedin.com/in/channy">Channy</a></p></content:encoded>

					<description>Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the […]</description>
										<content:encoded><p>Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/">AWS Lambda</a> learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/">Amazon S3</a> became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.</p> 
<p>The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…</p> 
<p><strong>Headlines</strong><br> <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/announcing-aws-lambda-web-functions-for-fast-consistent-web-app-performance-anywhere/">AWS Lambda Web Functions</a> is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run <code>aws lambda-web deploy</code>, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.</p> 
<p>Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding <code>--regions</code> to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/exploring-aws-lambda-web-functions-for-building-web-applications/">AWS Compute Blog</a> has a longer walkthrough, and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/">Amazon CloudFront</a> can now <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/cloudfront-lambda-web-functions-origin/">use a Web Function endpoint as an origin</a> with origin access control.</p> 
<p>The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/trust-in-depth-giving-agents-more-autonomy-without-losing-control/">Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control</a> makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/">Amazon Bedrock AgentCore</a> policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.</p> 
<p><strong>Last week’s launches</strong><br> Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-s3-vercel-marketplace-v0/">Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel</a> – You can now provision S3 general purpose buckets, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/features/tables/">S3 Tables</a>, and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/features/vectors/">S3 Vectors</a> from the Vercel dashboard, or by describing what you want to build in v0. It joins existing integrations for <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/rds/aurora/">Amazon Aurora</a>, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/">Amazon DynamoDB</a>, and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/features/serverless/">Amazon OpenSearch Serverless</a>, so the whole stack sits in one AWS account with one bill. The authentication detail is the good part: a short-lived OIDC token is exchanged at runtime with AWS Security Token Service for credentials scoped to that resource, so no static keys are stored anywhere.</li> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/ec2-t8i-instances-south-america/">Amazon EC2 T8i instances are now available in South America (São Paulo)</a> – The newest burstable generation reached the São Paulo Region, which matters for the unglamorous half of a workload: login gateways, small databases, CI/CD runners, low-traffic sites. <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/">Amazon EC2</a> T8i delivers up to 30 percent better price performance than T3, with up to 70 percent higher compute performance and 2.4 times the Amazon EBS bandwidth. It keeps the same CPU credit system as T3, so moving over is a size change rather than a redesign, and <code>t8i.micro</code> and <code>t8i.small</code> are available under the AWS Free Tier.</li> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-reflection-beam-an-open-weight-model-for-agentic-coding-on-aws/">Reflection Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding, is now on AWS</a> – You can now deploy Beam, Reflection AI’s open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks, from <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker-ai/jumpstart/">Amazon SageMaker JumpStart</a>. It’s a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 501 billion total and 23 billion active parameters, released on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0, and Reflection reports an effective context length of 1 million tokens. Start with a JumpStart real-time endpoint, or use <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker-ai/hyperpod/">SageMaker HyperPod</a> Inference with SGLang or vLLM when you need Kubernetes-native control. It was also <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/01/reflection-beam-on-sagemaker-jumpstart-and-aws-trainium/">ported and optimized for AWS Trainium3</a>, and launches in N. Virginia and Ohio.</li> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/aws-lambda-durable-go-sdk-support/">AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go is now generally available</a> – You can now write multi-step Go workflows that checkpoint their own progress and pause for up to a year while waiting on an external event, without building progress tracking yourself. That covers deployment rollouts with approval gates and pipelines that call a model and then stop for human review. It behaves like ordinary Go tooling: <code>go get</code> to add it, deploy a single static binary on the <code>provided.al2023</code> runtime, and test a full workflow locally with the <code>durabletest</code> package, no network access or credentials required.</li> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/cloudwatch-pipelines-log-routing/">Amazon CloudWatch announces log routing and chained log parsers</a> – You can now define routes in an <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/">Amazon CloudWatch</a> pipeline that send each event to a different log group based on conditions evaluated against processed fields, so severity, source, or event type can each land somewhere with its own retention and access controls. Chained parsers handle the other half: parsers run in sequence, with later ones consuming fields that earlier ones produced, so you can parse a JSON envelope first and then run a Grok parser over a field it extracted.</li> 
</ul> 
<p>For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/new/">What’s New with AWS</a> page.</p> 
<p><strong>Other AWS news</strong><br> Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-security-agent-now-part-of-aws-continuum-exploited-33-of-37-new-real-world-cves/">AWS Security Agent exploited 33 of 37 new real-world CVEs</a> – The team pointed their autonomous penetration-testing agent, now part of <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/continuum/">AWS Continuum</a>, at 37 recently disclosed CVEs packaged as live containerized targets, starting from nothing but an endpoint URL and a one-line hint. It captured 35 flags, and after auditing every win against the challenge’s canonical proof of concept, 33 of 37 (89.2 percent) held up as genuine end-to-end exploitation. The two misses are what make the post worth your time: in both, the agent found and exploited the bug, then took the target down before it could read the flag. A capable autonomous attacker is also a destructive one.</li> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/your-serverless-attendees-guide-to-aws-reinvent-2026/">Your serverless attendee’s guide to AWS re:Invent 2026</a> – A curated path through a very large catalog, worth having before the good sessions fill up.</li> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/how-dynata-scaled-ai-across-the-development-lifecycle-with-ai-dlc-and-kiro-ide/">How Dynata scaled AI across the development lifecycle with AI-DLC and Kiro IDE</a> – What changes when agentic coding stops being an individual habit and becomes how a team works.</li> 
</ul> 
<p><strong>Upcoming AWS events</strong><br> Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/events/reinvent/">AWS re:Invent</a> – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The <a href="https://registration.awsevents.com/flow/awsevents/reinvent2026/eventcatalog/page/eventcatalog">event catalog</a> is live and reserved seating is open, so <a href="https://registration.awsevents.com/flow/awsevents/reinvent2026/reg">register</a> and claim your spots before they fill up.</li> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/events/community-day/">AWS Community Days</a> – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. Here in Brazil, the 2026 season closes with <a href="https://awscommunityday.com.br/norte/">AWS Community Day Brasil Norte</a> in Belém on October 31, the final stop in a year that covered every region of the country for the first time.</li> 
</ul> 
<p>Join the <a href="https://builder.aws.com/build/capabilities?trk=f11c83db-08fa-4852-aa10-20185beeaef6&amp;sc_channel=el">AWS Builder Center</a> to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/events/">here</a> for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.</p> 
<p>That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!</p> 
<p>— Daniel Abib</p>

					<description>Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel.</description>
										<content:encoded><p>Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/">Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3)</a>, including <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/features/tables/">Amazon S3 Tables</a> and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/features/vectors/">Amazon S3 Vectors</a>, is natively available on the <a href="https://vercel.com/marketplace/aws">Vercel Marketplace</a> and <a href="https://v0.app/">v0 by Vercel</a>, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.</p> 
<p><strong>Why this matters</strong><br> Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/rds/aurora/">Amazon Aurora</a>, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/">Amazon DynamoDB</a>, and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/features/serverless/">Amazon OpenSearch Serverless</a>, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.</p> 
<p><strong>Storage for every application</strong></p> 
<ul> 
 <li><strong>S3 general purpose buckets</strong>: Store virtually unlimited objects, including files, images, videos, and documents, for data lakes, cloud-native applications, and mobile apps. S3 delivers the most durable storage in the cloud, designed to provide 99.999999999% (11 nines) data durability and 99.99% availability by default.</li> 
 <li><strong>S3 Tables</strong>: Fully managed Apache Iceberg storage optimized for analytics with automated table maintenance and compaction. S3 Tables are directly queryable from any Iceberg REST catalog API-compatible engine, including DuckDB.</li> 
 <li><strong>S3 Vectors</strong>: Purpose-built vector storage and query for AI applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and semantic search, reducing the cost of uploading, storing, and querying vectors by up to 90%.</li> 
</ul> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-105952" style="border: solid 1px #ccc" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/06/screenshot-1-vercel-marketplace-aws.jpg" alt="AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace with $100 in free AWS credits, serverless scale, and an Install button" width="1537" height="1026"></p> 
<p style="text-align: center"><em>Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.</em></p> 
<p><strong>Getting started</strong><br> From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.</p> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-106033" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/13/screenshot-2-create-resource-1.png" alt="" width="1306" height="1614"></p> 
<p style="text-align: center"><em>Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.</em></p> 
<p>Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:</p> 
<pre><code class="lang-bash">vercel link 
vercel env pull .env.local</code></pre> 
<p>The integration injects <code>AWS_REGION</code>, <code>AWS_ROLE_ARN</code>, <code>AWS_RESOURCE_ARN</code>, and a bucket name such as <code>S3_BUCKET_NAME</code>, <code>S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME</code>, or <code>S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME</code>. At runtime, the <code>awsCredentialsProvider</code> from <code>@vercel/functions/oidc</code> exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.</p> 
<p><strong>Object storage with S3</strong><br> This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:</p> 
<pre><code class="lang-javascript">import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { awsCredentialsProvider } from "@vercel/functions/oidc";

const s3 = new S3Client({
  region: process.env.AWS_REGION,
  credentials: awsCredentialsProvider({
    roleArn: process.env.AWS_ROLE_ARN,
  }),
});

export async function POST(request) {
  const formData = await request.formData();
  const file = formData.get("file");

  await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.S3_BUCKET_NAME,
    Key: file.name,
    Body: Buffer.from(await file.arrayBuffer()),
    ContentType: file.type,
  }));

  return Response.json({ success: true });
}</code></pre> 
<p>Use <code>ListObjectsV2Command</code> and <code>GetObjectCommand</code> with the same client to list and read objects.</p> 
<p><strong>Analytics with S3 Tables</strong><br> S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:</p> 
<pre><code class="lang-javascript">import { DuckDBInstance } from "@duckdb/node-api";
import { awsCredentialsProvider } from "@vercel/functions/oidc";

const creds = await awsCredentialsProvider({
  roleArn: process.env.AWS_ROLE_ARN,
})();

const db = await DuckDBInstance.create();
const conn = await db.connect();

await conn.run("INSTALL aws; LOAD aws; INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs; INSTALL iceberg; LOAD iceberg;");

await conn.run(`
  CREATE SECRET s3cred (
    TYPE s3,
    KEY_ID '${creds.accessKeyId}',
    SECRET '${creds.secretAccessKey}',
    SESSION_TOKEN '${creds.sessionToken}',
    REGION '${process.env.AWS_REGION}'
  );
`);

await conn.run(`
  ATTACH '${process.env.AWS_RESOURCE_ARN}' AS s3tables (
    TYPE iceberg,
    ENDPOINT_TYPE s3_tables
  );
`);

const rows = await (await conn.run(`
  SELECT town_city, AVG(median_price) AS avg_price
  FROM s3tables."${process.env.S3_TABLES_NAMESPACE}".town_monthly
  GROUP BY town_city
  ORDER BY avg_price DESC
  LIMIT 10
`)).getRowObjects();</code></pre> 
<p>If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add <code>@duckdb/node-api</code> to <code>serverExternalPackages</code> in <code>next.config.mjs</code> so the native bindings are not bundled.</p> 
<p><strong>Vector search with S3 Vectors</strong><br> S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:</p> 
<pre><code class="lang-javascript">import { S3VectorsClient, QueryVectorsCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3vectors";
import { awsCredentialsProvider } from "@vercel/functions/oidc";

const vectors = new S3VectorsClient({
  region: process.env.AWS_REGION,
  credentials: awsCredentialsProvider({
    roleArn: process.env.AWS_ROLE_ARN,
  }),
});

export async function POST(request) {
  const { embedding } = await request.json();

  const result = await vectors.send(new QueryVectorsCommand({
    vectorBucketName: process.env.S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME,
    indexName: "documents",
    queryVector: { float32: embedding },
    topK: 5,
    returnMetadata: true,
  }));

  return Response.json({ matches: result.vectors });
}</code></pre> 
<p><strong>Building with v0 by Vercel</strong><br> From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where users upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.</p> 
<p><img loading="lazy" class="aligncenter size-full wp-image-105950" style="border: solid 1px #ccc" src="https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/da4b9237bacccdf19c0760cab7aec4a8359010b0/2026/10/06/screenshot-4-v0-app.jpg" alt="v0 chat with the Amazon S3 Vectors integration connected and the generated PDF support bot application in the Preview panel" width="1646" height="959"></p> 
<p style="text-align: center"><em>Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.</em></p> 
<p><strong>Combining S3 with AWS databases</strong><br> Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.</p> 
<p><strong>Using Vercel with your AWS account</strong><br> You can create a new AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.</p> 
<p><strong>Pricing and availability</strong><br> There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit <a href="https://v0.app/">v0</a> or the AWS page on the <a href="https://vercel.com/marketplace/aws">Vercel Marketplace</a>.</p> 
<p><strong>Join the conversation</strong><br> If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/getting-started-aws-mcp-server.html">AWS MCP Server</a> and <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/plugins.html">plugins</a> with your preferred AI tool. Share your feedback on <a href="https://repost.aws/tags/TADSTjraA0Q4-a1dxk6eUYaw/amazon-simple-storage-service">AWS re:Post for Amazon S3</a>.</p> 
<p>— Daniel</p></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><p>Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/">Amazon ElastiCache</a> peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.</p> 
<p>The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/">Amazon Bedrock</a> at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…</p> 
<p><span id="more-105986"></span></p> 
<p><strong>Headlines</strong><br> <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/all-the-numbers-amazon-prime-day-2026-powered-by-aws/">All the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS</a> is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/">Amazon DynamoDB</a> processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/">AWS Lambda</a> handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ebs/">Amazon EBS</a> peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ecs/">Amazon ECS</a> launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/fargate/">AWS Fargate</a>, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/graviton/">AWS Graviton</a> powered up to 49 percent of the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/">Amazon EC2</a> compute that Amazon.com used.</p> 
<p>The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/fis/">AWS Fault Injection Service</a> experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/aws-countdown/">AWS Countdown Premium</a> is built for exactly that kind of planning.</p> 
<p><strong>Last week’s launches</strong><br> Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-claude-haiku-5-5-on-aws/">Claude Haiku 5.5 is now available on AWS</a> – You can now use the fastest model in the Claude 5.5 family on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS, at around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It’s the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence per task instead of fixing one setting for a whole workload. It pairs naturally with Claude Opus 5.5: Opus plans and makes the judgment calls, and because Haiku is fast and cheap, you can run many Haiku subagents in parallel for routing, classification, and small code changes across many files.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/amazon-nova-2.5-sonic/">Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic for voice agents</a> – You can now build real-time voice agents on a speech-to-speech <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/nova/">Amazon Nova</a> model with better reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, plus lower latency. That combination matters for multi-step work: a support agent can look up an order, check return eligibility, and start the return inside one conversation. It keeps expressive voices in seven languages, controllable turn-taking, and a 256K context window, and pairs with Strands Bidi Agents, <a href="https://strandsagents.com/blog/bidi-agents-now-ga/">now generally available</a>, to get a production voice agent going in a few lines of code.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/guardduty-rds-data-exfiltration/">Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection now detects data exfiltration and destruction</a> – <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/">Amazon GuardDuty</a> now looks past login anomalies to the queries themselves on <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/rds/aurora/">Amazon Aurora</a> PostgreSQL and <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/rds/">Amazon RDS</a> for PostgreSQL. RDS Protection for data activity builds behavioral baselines and uses ML-based anomaly detection plus threat intelligence to flag unusual data access, with no agents, extra infrastructure, or database configuration changes. This closes a real gap: once an attacker has valid credentials from phishing or a misconfiguration, their queries can look indistinguishable from your application’s.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/aws-Lambda-supports-oauth-kafka-esm/">AWS Lambda supports OAuth for self-managed Apache Kafka event sources</a> – You can now authenticate Lambda Kafka consumers through your enterprise identity provider, such as Amazon Cognito or Okta. Event source mappings previously supported only SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mTLS, which left teams in regulated industries unable to use Kafka ESM at all. Now you get the automatic scaling, batching, error handling, and event filtering of Kafka ESM with the same identity governance you apply everywhere else. It works with self-hosted clusters and managed offerings including Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/redshift-iceberg-materialized-views">Amazon Redshift adds Apache Iceberg materialized views</a> – You can now pre-compute expensive joins and aggregations once in <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/redshift/">Amazon Redshift</a> and store the result as an Iceberg table in <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/">Amazon S3</a>, registered in the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/glue/">AWS Glue</a> Data Catalog. You create them with familiar SQL, and the results are immediately queryable by any Iceberg-compatible engine, including <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/athena/">Amazon Athena</a>, Apache Spark, Trino, and Snowflake. Redshift keeps them current by recomputing only what changed. There’s a <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/materialize-once-query-anywhere-introducing-iceberg-materialized-views-in-amazon-redshift/">good deep dive on the AWS Big Data blog</a> if you want the details.</li> 
</ul> 
<p>For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/new/">What’s New with AWS</a> page.</p> 
<p><strong>Other AWS news</strong><br> Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/opensource/introducing-strands-box-ai-agent-sandboxes-powered-by-dogwood/">Introducing Strands Box: AI agent sandboxes powered by Dogwood</a> – As more of us let agents run shell commands and call APIs without approving every step, isolation alone stops being enough. <a href="https://github.com/strands-agents/box">Strands Box</a> is an open source sandbox (Apache 2.0, developer preview) that combines OS-level containment with fine-grained policies written in Dogwood, so permissions can depend on what the agent has already done. You can say “let the agent post to the incident channel, but no more than three times every 10 minutes” and have that enforced from outside the agent’s process. It also keeps real credentials out of the agent’s environment by attaching them at an egress gateway.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/aws-continuum-sets-a-new-standard-in-autonomous-code-security/">AWS Continuum sets a new standard in autonomous code security</a> – Related to that theme, AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/aws-continuum-penetration-testing/">now integrates into your CI/CD pipeline</a> in public preview, turning penetration testing into a deploy-time event instead of something that happens off to the side. Developers get findings with severity, affected endpoints, and remediation guidance right in the pipeline output, and the pipeline re-tests to verify fixes.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/how-postman-runs-agent-mode-for-40-million-developers-on-amazon-bedrock/">How Postman runs Agent Mode for 40 million developers on Amazon Bedrock</a> – A look at the architecture behind a feature serving a very large developer audience. Worth reading if you’re moving an agentic feature from a demo to something that has to hold up under real traffic.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/icymi-what-landed-for-ai-builders-in-september-2026/">ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026</a> – If you lost track of a month that included a lot of model launches, this is a tidy catch-up in one place.</li> 
</ul> 
<p><strong>Upcoming AWS events</strong><br> Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:</p> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/events/reinvent/" data-agent-id="141">AWS re:Invent</a> – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, and reserved seating is now open. The session catalog is live, so <a href="https://registration.awsevents.com/flow/awsevents/reinvent2026/reg" data-agent-id="142">register</a> and claim your spots in chalk talks, workshops, and builders’ sessions before they fill up.</li> 
</ul> 
<ul> 
 <li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/events/community-day/">AWS Community Days</a> – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, and this is a busy stretch. Upcoming stops include <a href="https://www.aws-aicd.com/">San Francisco</a> (October 13), <a href="https://awscommunitydaysoflo.com/">Miami</a> (October 14), <a href="https://awscommunitydayaus.com/">Brisbane</a> (October 16), <a href="https://www.awscommunityday.co.za/">Cape Town</a> (October 16), <a href="https://www.awscommunityday.mt/">Malta</a> (October 16), and <a href="https://acd.awsugmum.in/">Mumbai</a> (October 17). Here in Brazil, the <a href="https://awscommunityday.com.br/">community calendar</a> has more editions coming before the end of the year.</li> 
</ul> 
<p>Join the <a href="https://builder.aws.com/build/capabilities?trk=f11c83db-08fa-4852-aa10-20185beeaef6&amp;sc_channel=el">AWS Builder Center</a> to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/events/">here</a> for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.</p> 
<p>That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!</p> 
<p>– Daniel Abib</p> 
<p><em>This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!</em></p></content:encoded>

		<link>https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/announcing-aws-lambda-web-functions-for-fast-consistent-web-app-performance-anywhere/</link>
					
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Micah Walter]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 12 Oct 2026 22:34:47 +0000</pubDate>

					<description>AWS Lambda Web Functions is a serverless compute primitive that runs your HTTP framework natively, delivering fast, consistent responses through multi-concurrent execution and automated global distribution.</description>
										<content:encoded><p>Today, we’re announcing <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/lambda-web-functions/">AWS Lambda Web Functions</a>, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.</p> 
<p>With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.</p> 
<p><strong>Lambda Event Functions</strong> are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.</p> 
<p><strong>Lambda Web Functions</strong> use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.</p> 
<p><strong>Lambda MicroVMs</strong> provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.</p> 
<p>The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.</p> 
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Why Web Functions<br> </strong></span>Modern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.</p> 
<p>Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.</p> 
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Let’s try it out<br> </strong></span>To get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with <code>node index.js</code>, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.</p> 
<pre><code class="language-javascript">import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const [host, port] = process.env.AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT.split(':');

app.get('/', (req, res) =&gt; {
  res.json({ message: 'Hello from Lambda Web Functions!' });
});

app.listen(port, host, () =&gt; {
  console.log(`Server running on port ${port}`);
});
</code></pre> 
<p>The only difference from running locally is the <code>AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT</code> environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example <code>AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js</code>.</p> 
<p>With my code ready, I deployed using the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/cli/">AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)</a>:</p> 
<pre><code>aws lambda-web deploy --name my-web-app --code ./my-app
</code></pre> 
<p>One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.</p> 
<p>A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.</p> 
<p>I tested it immediately:</p> 
<pre><code>$ curl https://&lt;domain-id&gt;.&lt;shard-id&gt;.lambda-web.us-east-1.on.aws/
{"message":"Hello from Lambda Web Functions!"}
</code></pre> 
<p>Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:</p> 
<pre><code>aws lambda-web deploy --name my-web-app --code ./my-app \
    --regions us-east-1,eu-west-1,ap-northeast-1
</code></pre> 
<p>Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (<code>&lt;domain-id&gt;.lambda-web.global.on.aws</code>).</p> 
<p>When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.</p> 
<p>For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:</p> 
<pre><code>aws lambda-web update-web-function-endpoint \
    --function-name my-web-app \
    --endpoint-name dev \
    --auto-deployment-mode Disabled \
    --revision-weights '[{"revisionId": "&lt;current-revision-id&gt;", "weight": 90}, {"revisionId": "&lt;new-revision-id&gt;", "weight": 10}]'
</code></pre> 
<p>This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.</p> 
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Better together with Amazon CloudFront<br> </strong></span>For applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/">Amazon CloudFront</a>. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.</p> 
<p>Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront.&nbsp;With this launch, you attach CloudFront <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-origin.html">origin access control (OAC)</a> to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/s3/">Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3)</a>, without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.</p> 
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Now available<br> </strong></span>AWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.</p> 
<p>To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:</p> 
<pre><code>aws lambda-web deploy --name hello-world --hello-world
</code></pre> 
<p>For pricing details, visit the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/pricing/">AWS Lambda pricing page</a>. To learn more, see the <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/web-functions.html">Lambda Web Functions documentation</a>.</p></content:encoded>
